wpIntro: As a Doctor of Applied Health Research and data scientist, my career has been built on translating complex patterns into human-centred solutions. After years of bridging clinical data and patient experiences in UK cancer services, I’ve developed a singular curiosity:
wpQuestion: How do we narrate our own lives?
wpFollow: Follow as I experiment with applying analytical rigor to the architecture of everyday life, exploring how we build identity and belonging when we leave traditional, fixed structures behind.
reportIntro: I am a Doctor of Applied Health Research and trained data scientist with a background in population health data analytics. In 2024, I completed a mixed methods PhD at University College London exploring the utility of prescriptions data in improving early cancer detection in primary care in the UK. For the last three years I worked with cancer patients and clinicians to develop and improve UK cancer services tailored to the specific needs of teenagers and young adults. Bringing together data science and the lived experiences of patients and clinicians, I developed a strong interest in how people narrate and make sense of their lives. I developed this project as an experiment in extending that curiosity beyond academic and health systems research into everyday life and travel. It's also an experiment in bringing together skills in qualitative research and creativity. I call it the “home” project.
origin: While volunteering at Wonderland, I wanted to explore the construct of home through informal conversations with volunteers. Wonderland provides a uniquely rich environment for this exploration, as it brings together people from diverse cultural and geographic backgrounds who are temporarily sharing space and experiences.
impact: The project aims to generate both personal and communal value. For participants, the conversations may provide an opportunity for reflection and meaningful dialogue around identity, belonging, and place. For Wonderland, the project contributes to the intellectual and creative life of the community by fostering thoughtful conversations among volunteers. For the researcher, the project forms part of a broader transition from formal scientific research toward creative exploration of human experiences.
registers: This project produces at least three different kinds of output, deliberately not held to the same standard. There is knowledge: what the coded, transcript-grounded findings above actually support, requiring methodological transparency and bounded claims. There is literature: the essays and narrative writing this material could support, requiring craft and editorial judgement rather than representativeness. And there is art: the visual fingerprints discussed above, requiring aesthetic experimentation rather than evidentiary weight. Keeping these three registers distinct is a discipline the project owes itself, precisely because there is no institutional peer review enforcing the distinction from outside.
